hypotheses.title: Path Traversal
hypotheses.rationale: The use of `filepath.Base` is intended to prevent path traversal by extracting only the last element of the path. However, `filepath.Base` returns `..` if the input is `..` or ends with `..`. Consequently, an attacker can provide a query parameter `file=..`, which results in `filepath.Join('/srv/files', '..')` resolving to `/srv`, allowing the attacker to read the parent directory of the intended files directory.

hypotheses.title: Path Traversal
hypotheses.rationale: The application uses path.basename() to sanitize the user-provided filename. However, path.basename('..') returns '..', and path.basename('.') returns '.'. If an attacker provides '..' as the name parameter, path.join('/srv/files', '..') resolves to '/srv', allowing the attacker to traverse outside the intended base directory.

hypotheses.title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
hypotheses.rationale: The application reads the entire content of the requested file into memory using `fh.read()` without any size limit. If a user requests a very large file, this can lead to excessive memory consumption and potentially a Denial of Service (DoS) by exhausting the server's available RAM.

hypotheses.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via Port Manipulation
hypotheses.rationale: The application validates the hostname of the URL against a whitelist but does not validate the port. An attacker can specify an arbitrary port (e.g., 'https://images.example.org:1234'), allowing them to perform port scanning on the whitelisted hosts.

hypotheses.title: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (DoS)
hypotheses.rationale: The application accesses 'r.content', which loads the entire response body into memory. A malicious or compromised whitelisted host could send an extremely large response, leading to memory exhaustion and a Denial of Service (DoS).
